title: ASAP: Assembly-Source Aligned Pseudocode Refinement For Binary Decompilation
claim: Existing approaches use only lossy intermediate output or only raw low-level input; ours combines both to get the benefits of each.
layout: Top pipeline row, three dashed comparison boxes below, smiley pros/cons under each
description: The figure has two parts. The top is a black-and-white flow from Source Code to Binary (via a compiler such as GCC), then to Assembly (via a disassembler such as objdump). A decompiler such as Ghidra also takes the binary and produces Pseudocode. Each stage is a solid box with a small code snippet, a square function in this example. Below, three dashed boxes are numbered. (1) Pseudocode refinement: Pseudocode, then LLM, then Source. (2) End-to-end translation: Assembly, then LLM, then Source. (3) ASAP (ours): Assembly and Pseudocode both feed an LLM, then an assembly advantage loss, then Source, with alignment and masking boxes around the LLM. Each box ends with smiley and frowny faces marking pros and cons. The figure is monochrome with hollow arrows. The eye goes first to the top compilation chain, then to the numbered boxes.
caption: Comparison of our proposed \ASAP{} with existing binary decompilation approaches. The top shows the standard compilation and decompilation process from source code to binary, assembly, and decompiler-produced pseudocode. Below, three approaches are compared: (1) Pseudocode refinement takes decompiler output as input and improves it with an LLM; (2) End-to-end translation directly generates source code from assembly; (3) \ASAP{} augments the pseudocode refinement with assembly tokens, addressing the representation gap and attention bias.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in binary decompilation to refine the C-like pseudocode produced by traditional rule-based decompilers. While this pseudocode is useful, it is a heuristic and lossy abstraction rather than a faithful copy of the source code. It often contains decompiler errors, especially for aggressively optimized binaries where critical low-level details are obscured. We present ASAP, an Assembly-Source Aligned Pseudocode refinement framework for binary decompilation. ASAP learns source-aligned assembly representations from paired source and binary functions using joint function-level and snippet-level contrastive alignment. A Q-Former then compresses chunk-level assembly features into a fixed number of assembly tokens. These tokens and the decompiler-produced pseudocode jointly condition the decompilation LLM. During refinement, we use stochastic pseudocode masking and a relative assembly-advantage loss to discourage the model from relying solely on pseudocode. On two decompilation benchmarks across multiple compiler optimization levels, ASAP improves the average re-execution rate from 64.7% to 71.9% and the average recompilation rate from 91.6% to 96.6% compared with the strongest baseline. Our approach offers both a new perspective and a practical solution to binary decompilation.
